An audit into One Nation’s "Fire the Liar" fundraiser has concluded the millions of dollars it has received are legitimate, after questions were raised about the authenticity of donations.

A "functional audit" into One Nation’s "Fire the Liar" fundraiser has concluded the millions of dollars it has received are legitimate, after questions were raised about the authenticity of donations.

The seven-page examination was prepared by software developer Daryl Monnink on Thursday.

In the audit, obtained first by Sky News, Mr Monnink concludes that "based on the source code … SQL query review, inspection of sample production data and discussion held with (the donation code engineer), I am satisfied that the fundraising total calculation currently includes only successfully received and validated donation payments".

The donation drive is run through the party’s website, and does not list individual donors or amounts, as other websites such as GoFundMe tend to do.

However, the audit finds the figure displayed "excludes unpaid pledges, unvalidated transactions, BPAY and bank deposit pledges awaiting reconciliation, and future recurring donation amounts", indicating the value of donations will continue to rise as more get cleared through payment gateways, such as PayPal.

"The displayed fundraising total therefore represents actual funds received at the time of calculation rather than the total value of all donation pledges recorded within the system," the audit reads.

As of Thursday afternoon the campaign, which launched on Wednesday, has raised more than $2 million in its first two days.

At a press conference on Thursday morning, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the donations’ legitimacy into question.

When quizzed on what he made of the amount of money raised, the Prime Minister asked "what evidence is there?"

On the sidelines of an event in Western Australia, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson rubbished suggestions the figures have been fabricated.

"Why would I call out the liar … then go and do something like that myself? It would destroy me," Ms Hanson said.

"(The Prime Minister) can’t imagine One Nation getting the support we have. To get that amount of money says the Australian people have had a gutful of him."

Earlier, a One Nation official told Sky News there had been more than 28,000 individual donors through the website, each giving an average of $59.

The largest single donation, the official claims, was "around $15,000".

Current rules only require donations above $17,300 to be publicly disclosed. The threshold will come down to $5,000 from January next year.

Tech experts who have reviewed the audit have indicated to Sky News it is sufficient to instil confidence that the numbers One Nation has provided are accurate.

Its "Fire the Liar" campaign will be extended into the physical world over the next week.

The party has hired trucks brandishing the slogan to drive around Sydney and Melbourne, with stops planned outside the electorate offices of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Energy Minister Chris Bowen.

Party donations recently came under scrutiny, after Australia’s richest woman Gina Rinehart donated a million-dollar plane to its leader Pauline Hanson.

"Yes it was donated. Yes I'm super happy. Yes it's fast. Yes it's amazing … Yes it means I can visit more regional towns across the country more often", Ms Hanson posted on social media at the time.

She has defended her receipt of the plane by arguing it saves the taxpayer money.
